books.section: Topic 6.3 Westward Expansion: Social and Cultural Development
The End of Native American Independence
The Railroads and Developments in the West

primary_sources: Helen Hunt Jackson, A Century of Dishonor (1881)

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which Native peoples in the West were able to preserve their cultures and autonomy between 1865 and 1892.

documents.title: The Treaty of Fort Laramie
documents.source: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Article I, April 29, 1868. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A treaty between the United States and the Lakota, ending Red Cloud's War; shows the government still treating tribes as nations to bargain with.
documents.text: "From this day forward all war between the parties to this agreement shall forever cease. The government of the United States desires peace, and its honor is hereby pledged to keep it. The Indians desire peace, and they now pledge their honor to maintain it."

documents.title: Chief Joseph in Washington
documents.source: Chief Joseph, address in Washington, D.C., 1879, published in the North American Review. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Nez Perce leader speaking after his people's forced removal; shows a Native leader demanding equal treatment under the law.
documents.text: "Let me be a free man, free to travel, free to stop, free to work, free to trade where I choose, free to choose my own teachers, free to follow the religion of my fathers, free to talk, think and act for myself, and I will obey every law or submit to the penalty."

documents.title: Helen Hunt Jackson on citizenship as a cure
documents.source: Helen Hunt Jackson, A Century of Dishonor (1881), Introduction. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A reformer who exposed the government's record; shows even sympathetic reformers doubting that instant citizenship would save Native peoples.
documents.text: "To assume that it would be easy, or by any one sudden stroke of legislative policy possible, to undo the mischief and hurt of the long past, set the Indian policy of the country right for the future, and make the Indians at once safe and happy, is the blunder of a hasty and uninformed judgment. The notion which seems to be growing more prevalent, that simply to make all Indians at once citizens of the United States would be a sovereign and instantaneous panacea for all their ills and all the Government's perplexities, is a very inconsiderate one."

documents.title: The Dawes Severalty Act, Section 6
documents.source: Dawes Severalty Act, 24 Stat. 388, Section 6, February 8, 1887. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An act of Congress dividing reservations into individual allotments; shows citizenship offered as the reward for leaving tribal life.
documents.text: "And every Indian born within the territorial limits of the United States to whom allotments shall have been made under the provisions of this act, or under any law or treaty, and every Indian born within the territorial limits of the United States who has voluntarily taken up, within said limits, his residence separate and apart from any tribe of Indians therein, and has adopted the habits of civilized life, is hereby declared to be a citizen of the United States..."

documents.title: Richard Henry Pratt on the boarding schools
documents.source: Richard Henry Pratt, 'The Advantages of Mingling Indians with Whites,' address to the National Conference of Charities and Correction, Denver, 1892. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The founder of the Carlisle Indian School stating the assimilationist program; shows the schools' goal in the founder's own words.
documents.text: "A great general has said that the only good Indian is a dead one. In a sense, I agree with the sentiment, but only in this: that all the Indian there is in the race should be dead. Kill the Indian in him, and save the man."

documents.title: Wovoka's message
documents.source: Wovoka, 'The Messiah Letter,' as recorded by ethnologist James Mooney, 1891, published in The Ghost-Dance Religion and the Sioux Outbreak of 1890 (1896). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The Paiute prophet's message as carried to the Plains tribes; shows a spiritual answer to defeat, not a call to war.
documents.text: "Do not refuse to work for the whites and do not make any trouble with them until you leave them. ... When the time comes there will be no more sickness and everyone will be young again."

documents.title: Burial of the Lakota dead at Wounded Knee
documents.source: Photograph of the burial of Lakota dead at Wounded Knee, South Dakota, winter of 1890-1891. Public domain (Library of Congress via Wikimedia Commons).
documents.sourcing: A photograph of the burial party after the killing at Wounded Knee Creek; shows what the end of armed resistance looked like.
documents.text: The photograph shows men loading Lakota dead onto a wagon at Wounded Knee Creek, South Dakota, in the winter of 1890-1891, while soldiers on horseback watch from the ridge behind them.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which Native peoples preserved their cultures and autonomy between 1865 and 1892, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of preservation does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Civil War's end freeing the government to turn west, the railroad expansion across the Plains, or the long history of treaty-making with Native nations.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about Native cultures and autonomy.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876), the Nez Perce flight of 1877, the Indian Peace Commission of 1867, or the loss of the buffalo herds.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of preservation, showing that autonomy was lost while cultural identity survived in new forms, or explaining why the same policies produced different results for different peoples.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Between 1865 and 1892 Native peoples in the West lost nearly all of their political autonomy, yet they preserved their cultures in adapted forms, through armed resistance, legal appeals, and spiritual renewal, even as the government stripped away the land and institutions that had sustained them.
Context: The Civil War ended with the federal government holding a vast public domain and a railroad-building habit, while eastern industry demanded western land, and the Plains peoples who lived there became the obstacle to that demand.
Evidence: Document 1 shows the government still treating the Lakota as a nation in 1868, while Document 2 shows Chief Joseph, a decade later, asking only to be treated as a free man under the law. Documents 3 and 4 show the reformers' answer, allotment and citizenship, offered as a cure that Jackson herself doubted. Document 5 states the schools' goal in Pratt's own words, and Document 6 shows the spiritual answer, the Ghost Dance, while Document 7 shows where armed resistance ended, at Wounded Knee.
Beyond the documents: Little Bighorn in 1876 showed the Lakota could still win a battle, and the Nez Perce flight of 1877 showed a people choosing exile over surrender, while the destruction of the buffalo removed the economic base of Plains life.
Sourcing: The treaty and the Dawes Act show the government's purposes in its own words; Joseph and Wovoka speak for peoples under pressure; Jackson, a sympathetic outsider, warns that the reformers' cure may be another harm.
Complexity: Autonomy was lost almost entirely, yet culture survived in new forms. The Ghost Dance kept old hopes alive under a new religion, and Joseph's appeal to American law used the conqueror's own language to claim freedom.
